title: Coil-built snail sculpture in air-dry clay
subtitle: A decorative garden or shelf piece built from coils, no kiln required
excerpt: A coiled snail with a spiral shell and outstretched body built entirely from air-dry clay. The shell is formed by coiling in a flat spiral and lifting it onto a modelled body; the whole piece dries at room temperature and can be painted or sealed for indoor display.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Coil-building methods referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled between the palms, used as the building unit in coil construction
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to join and refine
Fully air-dried and unfired; fragile, ready for surface sealing
Clay diluted with water to a brushable or paste consistency, used as an adhesive for joining clay pieces

content.text: This snail uses the same
coil

technique that shaped some of the earliest ceramic vessels made: ropes of clay layered, joined, and smoothed into a finished form. No kiln is required. The piece dries at room temperature over two to three days and can sit on a shelf or garden windowsill once sealed.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay thinned with water to double cream consistency)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation
Keep the clay moist throughout. Work on a non-stick surface such as a piece of canvas or a silicone mat. Cover any clay you are not actively working with under a damp cloth. Mix a small amount of
slip
by scraping small scrapings of the same clay into a jar of water and stirring until the consistency matches double cream.
Building the body
Roll a flat oval shape from clay roughly 10 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 1.5 cm thick. This is the foot of the snail body. Smooth the underside flat with a wooden rib.

At one end of the oval, pinch and model a raised head shape roughly 3 cm high. Pinch out two small horn stalks from the top of the head, each about 1 cm long. Add small ball tips to the ends of each stalk for eyes.
Score a 3 cm circle on the top surface of the body behind the head using the needle tool. Roughen the scored area and apply slip to it. This is where the shell will attach.
Building the shell

Roll a long coil about 1 cm in diameter and 30 cm long. Starting from one end, coil it flat on the work surface in a tight spiral, pressing each round against the previous one. The base of the spiral should measure about 5 cm across.

Continue coiling upward on top of the flat base, placing each new coil directly on top of the previous layer and angling slightly inward so the shell tapers toward the top. Three or four rising coils of decreasing size complete a recognisable cone.
Smooth the outer surface with a barely damp sponge, blending the coil joins while preserving the spiral ridges if a textured look is wanted. Leave the base of the shell unsmoothed for now.

Score the base of the shell and apply slip. Press the shell onto the slipped area on the body at a slight backward tilt. Support the shell upright with a small wad of scrunched newspaper while the joint firms up. Do not leave the paper inside for more than an hour as the drying clay will grip it.
Drying
Leave the snail on a flat board at room temperature. Cover loosely with a plastic bag for the first 12 hours to slow drying and reduce cracking at the shell joint. The piece reaches
leather-hard
in 6 to 8 hours, at which point the horns and head can be refined with a needle tool. Full
bone-dry
takes 48 hours in a typical room. The piece is ready to seal when it feels pale, lightweight, and no cooler than the surrounding air.
Finishing

Apply two coats of diluted PVA to the whole surface, allowing each coat to dry fully. This seals the clay against minor moisture. Paint with acrylics once the PVA is dry: earthy browns and greens on the shell, a warm grey or ochre on the body. Leave the eye tips pale. A final coat of matte varnish gives a more durable finish than PVA alone.
Use and care
This piece is decorative only. Air-dry clay is not waterproof: keep indoors away from rain and condensation. Wipe with a dry cloth. Do not place on a damp surface.
Variations
Make a family of three snails at different scales: 15 cm, 10 cm, and 6 cm long. Arrange them climbing a painted branch on a wall panel.
Use paper-clay air-dry instead for a stronger body that is less likely to crack at the shell joint.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Shell detaches from body during drying
items.cause: The join surface was not scored and slipped thoroughly before attaching
items.fix: Reattach by scoring both surfaces, applying fresh slip, and pressing together. Hold for a minute and support with a small prop while it firms

items.cause: They dried faster than the main body because of their small mass and exposed surface
items.fix: Reattach with fresh slip once both parts are bone-dry. Wrap a damp cloth around the joint for a few hours to let it re-hydrate slightly before pressing together

items.problem: Coil joins are visible on the shell surface
items.cause: The coils were not smoothed while still soft
items.fix: At leather-hard, rub the joins with a damp finger or the rounded back of the needle tool to blend them. The spiral groove between coils can be left or smoothed to taste

items.problem: Shell leans to one side as it dries
items.cause: The shell was attached at too steep an angle or the base scored area was too small
items.fix: Prop with a small wad of tissue or foam until the join is firm enough to hold the shell upright
